rationale: The 26-week executive mean nominally favors high-oleic sunflower oil against either fish-oil dose, with an inconclusive difference and different 13-week ordering. Attention changes favor the active comparators. No oil-free arm, confirmed cold pressing, or Parkinson cohort.

Exploratory switching at six months was 81.1 s versus 110.1 s on coconut oil (p=.037); the within-sunflower comparison was p=.07. The supplier specification is physically refined, with no historical lot certificate. Parkinson was excluded; 31 randomized, endpoint denominator and transfer remain limited.

Refined sunflower switching moved from 130 to 131 seconds with an inconclusive arm difference. Trail Making total errors went from 1.7 to 2.5 versus 2.7 to 1.8 on MCT (adjusted p=.017). OC5 describes this same MCI family. No cold-pressed or oil-free comparison.

Relative to high-oleic sunflower, DHA shortened the composite working-memory response time by 0.36 SD (95% CI 0.14 to 0.58). This shows the relative assigned diets, with an uncertain preparation and no oral sunflower-only or Parkinson estimate.
High-oleic sunflower capsules served as active comparator for conjugated linoleic acid. Trail Making and Serial Sevens yielded no clear between-arm change. No cold pressing or Parkinson cohort.

An acute high-oleic sunflower meal produced better discrimination than a high-saturated-fat meal (p=.02). A single-meal attention comparison and multiple changing fats do not identify chronic executive impairment or an oil-alone intervention.
Sunflower frequency corresponded to +2 total PRO-PD points per frequency level (95% CI −10 to 13). A cross-sectional composite assessment did not isolate the executive symptom or pressing grade.

Images, numbers and words were recalled better after 29 days. The single-cohort before-and-after format does not control for practice and the accessible abstract lacks dosing mass, pressing grade or a distinct executive task.

Oral sunflower seed oil improved novel-object discrimination at both doses versus water in scopolamine-treated mice, both p<.001. The preparation is unverified and the model tests recognition memory without a Parkinson mechanism or executive task.

Both high-fat arms had poorer chronic spatial maze performance. A standard chow contrast changes dietary fat and energy, and there is no conventional-fat sunflower group or Parkinson disease pathology. The oil processing is unverified.

Figure 2 shows sunflower and chow near overlapping. The omnibus result and saturated-arm caption cannot assign a signed sunflower contrast. Author overlap with the original ECO member and later high-fat work leaves the experiment lineage open.

The progressive dopaminergic-loss experiment tests behavior after common tamoxifen injection in sunflower oil. There is no edible exposure contrast or separate executive measure. The later gene-expression report uses the same model but a different schedule.
Rotenone in carrier was contrasted with carrier. The difference in social recognition is a toxin-model observation; injection, common oil and different task prevent sunflower attribution.

The combined saline plus oral oil vehicle made more working-memory errors at 72 hours than untreated controls (p=.0127). Additional reference-memory errors occurred at 72 and 96 hours. The handling and saline schedule, no pressing grade and the non-Parkinson control comparison leave no transferable sign.
The reported culinary oil use has no measured neurologic outcome. Separate medicinal or ceremonial uses of the plant are contextual and do not supply an independent oil effect.
